'''Johann Carl "John" Vogel''' (7 September 1932 – 30 January 2012) was a South African isotope physicist with a specific interest in archeology for which he used [[radiocarbon dating]] to establish timeframes.

==Career==
Vogel was born on 7 September 1932 in [[Pretoria]].<ref name="quat">{{cite web|last1=Wintle|first1=Ann|last2=Jacobs|first2=Zenobia|author-link2=Zenobia Jacobs|last3=Talma|first3=Siep|date=20 February 2012|title=Johann Carl Vogel (7 September 1932–30 January 2012)|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257700682|accessdate=31 January 2016|publisher=Quaternary Geochronology}}</ref> He obtained a BSc in chemistry in 1951, and a MSc in 1955, both from the [[University of Pretoria]]. He moved to Germany to study at [[Heidelberg University]] where he obtained a doctorate under [[Otto Haxel]] in 1959. The subject of his thesis was determination of carbon isotope fractionation factors.<ref name=quat/><ref name=sajs>{{cite web|author=Graham Baker |url=http://www.sajs.co.za/sites/default/files/publications/pdf/1419-10589-1-PB.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170811080032/https://www.sajs.co.za/sites/default/files/publications/pdf/1419-10589-1-PB.pdf |title=Johann Carl Vogel: Chronologist (1932–2012) |publisher=South African Journal of Science |date=2012 |number=9 |archive-date=11 August 2017}}</ref><ref name=rug>{{cite web|url=http://www.rug.nl/research/portal/files/2460172/2012RadiocarbonTalma.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211228170136/https://pure.rug.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/2460172/2012RadiocarbonTalma.pdf |title=Obituary: Johann Carl Vogel (1932–2012) |publisher=University of Groningen |date=2012 |archive-date=28 December 2021}}</ref>

In 1961 Vogel wanted to move back to South Africa, but there being no suitable job available for him he instead moved to the Netherlands and obtained the position of head of the Radiocarbon Dating Laboratory at the [[University of Groningen]]. The position had become available after the death of [[Hessel de Vries]]. Vogel later became a professor of isotope geology at Groningen.<ref name=sajs/>

In 1967 Vogel returned to South Africa and set up a laboratory at the [[Council for Scientific and Industrial Research]] in Pretoria. Vogel was head of the Quaternary Dating Research Unit until 1997, when he retired.<ref name=rug/> During his career he developed techniques for dating unburnt bone and contributed to radiocarbon dating programmes.<ref name=saac>{{cite web |last1=Sievers |first1=C |url=https://www.archaeology.org.za/news/2012/February/pioneer-radiocarbon-dating-passes |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230929081619/https://www.archaeology.org.za/news/2012/February/pioneer-radiocarbon-dating-passes |title=Pioneer of radiocarbon dating passes on |publisher=South African Archaeological Society |date=2 February 2012 |archive-date=29 September 2023}}</ref> 

From 1986 to 1988 he was President of the [[South African Archaeological Society]].<ref name=saac/> In 1988, Vogel received the De Beers Gold Medal from the [[South African Institute of Physics]] in 1988.<ref name=quat/> He was a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of South Africa]].<ref name=quat/>

Vogel was married to Ursula Weidemann, a professor of Ancient History at the [[University of South Africa]].<ref name=sajs/> He died on 30 January 2012.<ref name=quat/>
